passage: I'm Salma, and I sat in on the review after the website went down on Saturday. I braced for names. Hemant, who led it, began differently: "We're here to understand how it unfolded. Nobody is on trial." Hemant wrote three questions on the whiteboard: What went wrong? What made that possible? What would stop it happening again? The engineer who had pushed the change spoke first, calmly, because nobody had pointed a finger. We found the update went out at five on Friday with no second reviewer on call, and the warning alert went to an inbox nobody watched. By the end we had two fixes: a second-reviewer rule and alerts sent to phones. Nobody's job was in question. I left feeling lighter.

qa.q: What three questions did Hemant write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Hemant wrote: What went wrong? What made that possible? What would stop it happening again?

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as the review began?
qa.a: Braced and worried that names would be blamed.

qa.q: What two fixes came out of the review?
qa.a: A second-reviewer rule and alerts sent to phones.

qa.q: Why did the engineer who pushed the change speak calmly?
qa.a: Nobody had pointed a finger, so it felt safe to say what happened.

grounding: Shows a team reviewing a failure by asking what happened and what conditions allowed it, fixing the system rather than the person.

passage:
Tuesday. A shipment of 300 cartons went to the wrong city. Charu, who had entered the address, said nothing and went white. Madhav, the team lead, said only, "We'll meet on Thursday and work out what happened. Nobody will be blamed."

Thursday. At the meeting Madhav asked three questions: what happened, what allowed it, what would prevent it. Charu explained: two city codes looked almost the same in the drop-down list, and there was no second check. The team saw the pattern, not just the person.

Next Tuesday. The form showed the city name beside each code, and a second person confirmed every entry. Charu keyed in the next order, breathing easier, and a colleague signed the check.

qa.q: How many cartons went to the wrong city?
qa.a: Three hundred cartons went to the wrong city.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling on Tuesday when the shipment error came out?
qa.a: Frightened and ashamed, shown by going white and saying nothing.

qa.q: Which changes prevented a repeat?
qa.a: Showing the city name beside each code and having a second person confirm every entry.

qa.q: How does Madhav's approach differ from hunting for a culprit?
qa.a: Madhav asked what allowed the error and what would prevent it, so the team saw the system problem, not only the person.

grounding: Shows a lead running a blameless look at a failure that fixes the conditions rather than punishing the person.

passage:
Zeenat, you're running the print unit now. Let your Zubin chacha tell you about the wedding card disaster.
Years ago, we printed five hundred wedding cards with the wrong date. The family was furious. My first instinct was to find out who did it and shout.
Instead, the next morning, I sat my four workers down with chai and asked three questions. What happened? What made it possible? What would stop it next time?
It came out slowly. The customer had changed the date by phone. Raju took the call but was busy, and wrote it on a scrap. The designer never saw the scrap. The proof went to the family with the old date, and they didn't notice either.
Nobody was careless, beta. The system had no place for a phone change.
We made one rule: every change in writing, signed by the customer on the proof. We never printed a wrong date again.

qa.q: How many wedding cards were printed with the wrong date?
qa.a: Five hundred wedding cards.

qa.q: What was Zubin's first instinct, and how did he feel about it?
qa.a: Zubin felt angry and wanted to find the culprit and shout, but he chose to hold that back.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking what happened, what allowed it and what would prevent it, because it showed the gap was the missing system for phone changes, not one careless person.

qa.q: How might Raju have felt during the chai meeting?
qa.a: Raju was probably nervous at first, expecting blame, then relieved when the conversation focused on the process.

grounding: An elder recalls a review that asked what happened and what allowed it, fixing the system instead of blaming a person.

passage:
The school's annual day had ended ten minutes early when the sound system failed. Three hundred parents had left grumbling. Now, at 9 p.m., with the principal expecting a report by morning, Binita, the events coordinator, sat with her team in the empty hall.
Zubin, the technician, sat stiffly, arms crossed. He clearly expected to be blamed.
"I'm not looking for who," Binita said. "I want to know what happened. Walk me through it."
Zubin uncrossed his arms. The main amplifier had overheated. It was placed behind the curtain, with no air. The rented spare was in the storeroom, and the key was with the peon, who had gone home at eight.
"So what let it happen?" Binita wrote on the whiteboard: no airflow, spare locked away, no key plan.
"And what stops it next time?"
By 10:30 the list had three fixes. Binita's report named none of the team. Zubin helped her type it.

qa.q: Where was the main amplifier placed?
qa.a: It was placed behind the curtain, with no air.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel at the start of the meeting?
qa.a: Zubin felt tense and defensive, arms crossed, expecting to be blamed.

qa.q: Which approach did Binita use, and why did it work?
qa.a: Binita asked what happened, what allowed it and what would stop it, focusing on conditions, so Zubin could share the real causes.

qa.q: How might the principal read Binita's report?
qa.a: The principal would likely find it useful and fair, since it names the conditions and three fixes rather than a culprit.

grounding: Shows a team reviewing a failure by asking what happened and what conditions allowed it, fixing the system rather than blaming a person.

passage:
At the restaurant's Kochi branch, forty online orders on Sunday night had gone to a kitchen that was closed for repairs. Customers waited, then cancelled. The owner wanted names.
Sangeeta, the branch manager, called a review on Monday. Sahil, who had joined three weeks ago, came in pale. He had been on the order screen that night.
Sangeeta put a sheet on the table with three headings: What happened. What made it possible. What stops it.
Sahil explained: the ordering app showed the closed kitchen as open. He had noticed orders not being accepted but thought it was slow internet.
Others added: the closure had been told to staff by voice, not entered in the system. Nobody owned updating it. There was no alarm for unaccepted orders.
Under "What stops it," they wrote: a closure checklist, one owner for the online status, an alert after five unaccepted orders.
When Sahil left, his shoulders had come down.

qa.q: How many online orders went to the closed kitchen?
qa.a: Forty online orders.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel coming in to the review?
qa.a: Sahil felt frightened and pale, expecting to be blamed because he had been on the order screen.

qa.q: What did the review's third heading produce?
qa.a: A closure checklist, one owner for the online status and an alert after five unaccepted orders.

qa.q: How might the owner see the review's results?
qa.a: The owner wanted names, but may come to value fixes that prevent the problem instead of punishing one new worker.

grounding: Illustrates a manager who runs a blameless review, asking what happened and what allowed it, and fixes the system instead of the person.

passage:
"Okay, Saturday's deliveries," Binita said, pen at the whiteboard. "Thirty families got nothing. Let's start with what happened, step by step."
Nilesh shifted in his chair. "I had the old route sheet. That's on me."
"Hold on. I'm not looking for who. Why was the old sheet in the van at all?"
"It was on the clipboard. The new one was only in the group chat."
Mariam added, "And that message came at midnight. Most drivers leave at seven without checking."
"So, the conditions," Binita said, writing. "Two versions of the route, one on paper, one on a phone. Nobody confirming which. What would stop it happening again?"
"One sheet only. The old one goes in the bin when the new one's printed," Nilesh said.
"And a quick call at seven where drivers read out their first stop," Mariam said.
Binita underlined both. "Good. Nilesh, will you print the sheets from now on? You've seen exactly where it breaks."
Nilesh nodded, his shoulders dropping.

qa.q: How many families got no delivery on Saturday?
qa.a: Thirty families got nothing.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he said "That's on me"?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty and braced for blame; his shoulders dropping at the end show relief once the focus moved to the system.

qa.q: What two changes did the team agree on?
qa.a: Keep one printed route sheet and bin the old one, and hold a quick seven o'clock call where drivers read out their first stop.

qa.q: What would change if Binita had accepted "That's on me" and moved on?
qa.a: The team would have blamed Nilesh and missed the real cause, two versions of the route and a midnight message, so it could happen again with another driver.

grounding: Shows a team reviewing a failure by asking what happened and what conditions allowed it, fixing the process instead of hunting a culprit.
